name: Chest fly
angleNote: Horizontal adduction: 0° = arms out to the sides in line with the shoulders, 90° = arms pointing straight forward. Negative = arms behind the shoulders (stretch). Top view: x out to the side, y forward.
jointNote: Not truly one joint: as the arms come together the shoulder blades slide forward round the rib cage (protraction), and they draw back in the stretch. The model treats the arm as turning about one fixed shoulder point; how much of the motion the shoulder blade takes in a fly hasn't been checked here (TODO: source), and the shoulder-blade muscles (serratus anterior, rhomboids) aren't analysed.

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end, from de Leva's adjusted Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov table (young adult males). The forearm segment includes the hand (combined centre of mass along elbow → grip).
segments.massSource: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
segments.note: Shoulder→elbow and elbow→grip centre in metres. The arm is modelled straight; a fly is usually done with a soft elbow, which shortens the lever.

strengthCurve.label: Horizontal adductor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative horizontal-adduction strength vs arm angle (0° = arms out in line with the shoulders): constant from 30° behind that line to 60° in front, then a sharp drop (Williams & Stutzman, 10 men; Whitley, 31 men, found no change over 60°; both via Kulig et al.). How far it drops by 90–120° isn't given numerically, so those values are estimates.
strengthCurve.source: Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (shape; drop beyond 60° estimated)

muscles.name: Pectoralis major
muscles.source: Campos YAC, Vianna JM, Guimarães MP, Oliveira JLD, Hernández-Mosqueira C, da Silva SF, Marchetti PH (2020). J Hum Kinet 75:5–14. doi:10.2478/hukin-2020-0033 (13 men, 60% 1RM, % of maximal isometric activation)

muscles.name: Anterior deltoid
muscles.note: Assists horizontal adduction. 19% of maximum at 60% 1RM, the same as in the bench press (Campos et al.).

muscles.note: Helps hold the soft elbow bend under load.

phases.name: Stretch
phases.text: Arms wide. Lying with dumbbells this is the hardest point; standing at cables it is loaded too.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: Dumbbell torque falls with the cosine of the angle.

phases.name: Arms together
phases.text: Lying with dumbbells the weights are over the shoulders and almost unloaded; cables and machines still pull here.

variants.name: Flat dumbbell fly
variants.notes: Lying on your back, the arms move in a vertical plane: torque = m·g·L·cos(angle), largest with the arms out wide and zero with them overhead.

variants.name: Standing cable fly (pulleys at shoulder height)
variants.notes: Standing, the arms move in a horizontal plane, so gravity has no torque in this plane (it still has to be held up, which this 2D model ignores). The cable keeps tension with the arms together.

variants.name: Pec deck machine

camProfiles.label: Linkage machine (1989 patent)
camProfiles.note: Effective radius in metres: joint torque per unit of stack weight. The designer's computed curve for a pec deck driven by a four-bar linkage instead of a cam (US patent 4,840,373, FIG. 4, read off every 10°): the force at the arm pads rises from 97% of the stack weight to 121% at mid-range and falls steeply to 68% as the arms close. The pads start 20° behind the shoulder line and turn 110°, the same range as here, so pad rotation 10° = −10° here. Torque = that force × the pad distance (0.28 m here; the patent's pad radius isn't stated). Held flat before 10° of rotation (not plotted).
camProfiles.source: Maag HH (1989). Four-bar rigid-drive variable resistance pectoral fly machine. US Patent 4,840,373 (FIG. 4: force at the arm pads as % of the stack weight vs pad rotation, from the designer's kinematic analysis)

camProfiles.label: Rising cam (estimate)
camProfiles.note: Effective radius in metres: joint torque per unit of stack weight. A 1983 check of a Nautilus chest fly found the resistance rising through most of the movement (Harman, cam radii from photographs, no numbers published), and one maker describes its pec deck cam as progressively increasing (Panatta). How much it rises isn't published: here about 40% from the stretch to mid-range, then flat, an estimate.
camProfiles.source: Harman E (1983). Resistive torque analysis of 5 Nautilus exercise machines. Med Sci Sports Exerc 15(2):113. doi:10.1249/00005768-198315020-00117 (conference abstract; cam radii from photographs); Panatta (manufacturer product descriptions, read 2026-10-14: Fantastic Vertical Pek Dek, "progressively increasing" resistance; Standing Abductor, "decreasing" resistance in the lifting phase; no numbers given)

camProfiles.label: Round pulley (constant)
camProfiles.note: A plain round pulley: the lever between the belt and the axle never changes, so the resistance torque is the same at every angle (physics, no source needed). Many plate-loaded and budget machines work like this. Radius 0.30 m, nominal (stack kg don't compare between machines).
camProfiles.source: Physics: a round pulley's radius is constant (no source needed)

variants.notes: Seated, arms moving in a horizontal plane against pads at the elbows. The illustrative cam keeps the resistance fairly even across the range.
